explanations.answer: The priest sets a price they can afford
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The person is presented before the priest, who sets the value according to what the one making the vow can afford (Leviticus 27:8). The list has prices, but it also has room for an empty pocket. Nobody gets turned away at the door of this bakery over a few missing coins.

explanations.answer: The vow is canceled at no cost
explanations.explanation: I get the kind thought, friend, but that's not what the text says. The one making the vow is too poor to pay the valuation, so he presents the person before the priest. Then the priest sets the value according to what he can afford. The vow still stands, and the price just fits the person.

explanations.answer: A neighbor pays the full price for them
explanations.explanation: Nice neighbor, friend, but no neighbor shows up in this verse. The text says the one making the vow presents the person before the priest. The priest then sets the value according to what the one making the vow can afford. Same person, smaller price.
Yes, friend. Verse 9 says any such animal given to the LORD shall be holy. Once it's vowed, it's not just another animal in the pen anymore. It belongs to the LORD.

Close to a word that does show up in this chapter, friend, but not here. For this kind of animal, verse 9 says any such animal given to the LORD shall be holy. Selling comes up later for a different animal, in Leviticus 27:27. Here the word is holy.

Nope, nothing gets let go in this verse, friend. A vowed animal that may be brought as an offering isn't set loose to wander off. Verse 9 says any such animal given to the LORD shall be holy. Holy is the word to remember.

I know the thought, friend: trade up, everybody wins. But the text shuts that door. It says, “He must not replace it or exchange it, either good for bad or bad for good.” (Leviticus 27:10) A vowed animal stays the vowed animal, even if the new one looks better.

That's right, friend. The text says, “He must not replace it or exchange it, either good for bad or bad for good.” (Leviticus 27:10) That covers swapping up as well as swapping down. Once the animal is vowed, no trading.

You've got it, friend. Verse 10 says, if he does substitute one animal for another, both that animal and its substitute will be holy. So the swap doesn't get him out of anything. It just adds a second animal to the LORD's side of the pen.

Almost, friend, but the text goes further. Leviticus 27:10 says that if he substitutes one animal for another, both that animal and its substitute will be holy. The first animal stays holy, and so does the new one. He can't leave one behind in the swap.

Not quite, friend. Leviticus 27:10 says both that animal and its substitute will be holy. The first animal doesn't lose its place just because a new one stepped in. Two animals end up holy, and the swap gets him nothing.

Fair guess, friend, since it's his animal. But the text hands the pricing to someone else. Verse 11 says the animal must be presented before the priest, and verse 12 says the priest shall set its value, whether high or low. The owner doesn't get to name the number.

Right, friend. The animal is presented before the priest, and the priest shall set its value, whether high or low (Leviticus 27:11-12). As the priest values it, the price will be set. The owner doesn't get to haggle his own number.

That's the one, friend. Verse 13 says that if the owner decides to redeem the animal, he must add a fifth to its value. So buying it back costs a little more than the priest's price. One more piece on top, and the animal is his again.

Tenth is a real number in this chapter, friend, just not in this verse. Leviticus 27:13 says the owner must add a fifth to the value to redeem the animal. The tenth shows up later with the herd and the shepherd's rod (Leviticus 27:32). For buying back, count one fifth.
A third would cost more than the text asks, friend. Verse 13 says that if the owner decides to redeem the animal, he must add a fifth to its value. A fifth is what it takes. Keep that fraction handy.

explanations.answer: By the years left until the next Jubilee
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Verse 18 says the priest calculates the price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee, so that the valuation will be reduced. Fewer years left means a lower price. It's like a lease that runs shorter every year.

explanations.answer: By how big last year's harvest was
explanations.explanation: Sensible guess, friend, but the verse doesn't mention any harvest. Leviticus 27:18 says the priest calculates the price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee. As the Jubilee gets closer, the valuation is reduced. The calendar sets the price here.

explanations.answer: By what the owner first paid for it
explanations.explanation: That would make sense at a yard sale, friend, but this verse counts something else. It says the priest calculates the price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee, so that the valuation will be reduced. Nothing is said about what the owner first paid. The years left decide it.

explanations.answer: No it can no longer be redeemed
explanations.explanation: Correct, friend. Verse 20 says that if he does not redeem the field, or if he has sold it to another man, it may no longer be redeemed. The door closes, and there's no knocking on it afterward. It's like a cookie sale where the last batch sells out and you're standing there with an empty box, still saying, "But I wanted one!" So the time to buy it back is while he still can.

explanations.answer: Yes by adding a fifth to its value
explanations.explanation: The fifth is a good thing to remember, friend, but it only works while the owner still has the right to redeem. In verse 19, the one who consecrated the field decides to redeem it and adds a fifth. This card describes the other case. Verse 20 says that if he does not redeem it, or has sold it to another man, it may no longer be redeemed.

explanations.answer: Yes once the Year of Jubilee comes
explanations.explanation: Jubilee does come into the picture, friend, but not as a way to redeem it. Verse 20 says the field may no longer be redeemed. When it's released in the Jubilee, it becomes holy, like a field devoted to the LORD, and it becomes the property of the priests (Leviticus 27:21).

Yes, friend. Verse 21 says that when the field is released in the Jubilee, it will become holy, like a field devoted to the LORD. It becomes the property of the priests. This follows from verse 20, where the field was never redeemed or was sold to another man.

I know, friend, it sounds like a trick question. A field going to the priests? But read it slowly. Leviticus 27:21 says that when the field is released in the Jubilee, it will become holy, like a field devoted to the LORD, and it becomes the property of the priests. That's the field from verse 20, the one not redeemed or sold to another man, so the statement is True.

That's the one, friend. Verse 24 says that in the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought, the original owner of the land. The man consecrated a field he bought, so it goes back to where it came from.

The priests do get a field in this chapter, friend, but a different one. Leviticus 27:21 is about a field that was never redeemed or was sold. This card is about a field the man bought and consecrated. For that one, verse 24 says it shall return to the one from whom it was bought, the original owner of the land.

An oldest son never shows up in these verses, friend. Leviticus 27:24 says that in the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought. That's the original owner of the land. So the text sends it back to him, and a son isn't part of the picture.

explanations.answer: It already belongs to the LORD
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. Verse 26 says no one may consecrate a firstborn of the livestock, because a firstborn belongs to the LORD. Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is the LORD's. You can't give someone something that's already theirs.

explanations.answer: It is too young to be offered
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, friend, but the verse gives a different reason. Leviticus 27:26 says no one may consecrate a firstborn of the livestock, because a firstborn belongs to the LORD. Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is the LORD's. Age isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: It belongs to the oldest son
explanations.explanation: No oldest son in this verse, friend. The reason is that a firstborn belongs to the LORD, and the text says whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is the LORD's (Leviticus 27:26). That's why nobody can consecrate it.

That's right, friend. Verse 27 says that if the firstborn is among the unclean animals, he may redeem it according to the valuation and add a fifth of its value. If it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to the valuation. Redeem it or it's sold.

Letting it go sounds friendly, friend, but that's not what verse 27 says. The owner may redeem the unclean firstborn by adding a fifth. If it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to the valuation. There's no setting it loose.

That's a lot heavier than this verse, friend. Leviticus 27:27 says an unclean firstborn may be redeemed according to the valuation with a fifth added. If it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to the valuation. Sold is the word.

I understand the thought, friend, since the fifth worked for the other items. But devoted things are different. Verse 28 says nothing that a man sets apart to the LORD from all he owns can be sold or redeemed. Everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD.

Right, friend. The fifth doesn't work here. Verse 28 says that whether it's a man, an animal, or his inherited land, nothing set apart to the LORD can be sold or redeemed. Everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD.
Yes, friend. Verse 30 says any tithe from the land, whether from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD. It is holy to the LORD. The tithe is His from the start.

It grew on his land, so I see the thinking, friend. But the verse says otherwise. Leviticus 27:30 says any tithe from the land, from the seed or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD. It is holy to the LORD.

The town elders don't show up in this verse, friend. I think it's easy to picture somebody local collecting, but the text only names one owner. Leviticus 27:30 says the tithe from the land, whether from seed or from the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD. It is holy to the LORD. So the answer is Him, and no committee needed.

That's it, friend. Verse 32 says every tenth animal from the herd or flock that passes under the shepherd's rod will be holy to the LORD. Every tenth one that passes under the rod belongs to Him. The shepherd just keeps counting.

The fifth is all over this chapter, friend, so I get why it came to mind. But that's for adding to a price when you buy something back. Verse 32 says every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's rod will be holy to the LORD. Different job, different number.

Seventh is close in sound, friend, but it's not the number here. Leviticus 27:32 says every tenth animal from the herd or flock that passes under the shepherd's rod will be holy to the LORD. So the shepherd counts one, two, all the way to ten. That tenth one is the LORD's.

I see how it sounds like a fair move, friend, but the text blocks it. It says, “He must not inspect whether it is good or bad, and he shall not make any substitution.” (Leviticus 27:33) The tenth animal stays the tenth animal, whatever it looks like.
Right, friend. The text says, “He must not inspect whether it is good or bad, and he shall not make any substitution.” (Leviticus 27:33) No peeking, no picking. The tenth animal is the tenth animal.
